description: This classic Chinese breakfast features a silky smooth rice porridge, simmered to perfection and infused with savory flavors. Velvety congee is studded with distinctive century egg, offering a unique umami depth and creamy texture. It is a comforting and nourishing dish, perfect to start any day.

instructions.title: Prepare the Rice
instructions.text: Rinse the jasmine rice thoroughly under cold water until the water runs clear. Drain well. For best results, soak the rice in 2 cups of water for at least 30 minutes, or overnight in the refrigerator. This helps the grains break down faster for a smoother congee.

instructions.title: Prepare Century Eggs and Pork
instructions.text: Carefully peel the century eggs and dice them into small, bite-sized pieces. If using pork, shred it finely and marinate with a pinch of salt, a dash of white pepper, and 1 teaspoon of cornstarch for 10 minutes. This will keep the pork tender.

instructions.title: Start the Congee Base
instructions.text: In a large pot, combine the soaked and drained rice with 8 cups of water or chicken broth and the sliced ginger. Bring the mixture to a rolling boil over high heat, then immediately reduce the heat to low. Cover the pot, leaving a small gap for steam to escape, and simmer.

instructions.title: Simmer the Congee
instructions.text: Continue to simmer the congee on low heat for 30-40 minutes, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking and to ensure even cooking. The rice grains should break down and become very soft, creating a thick, creamy porridge consistency. If it becomes too thick, add a little more hot water or broth.

instructions.title: Add Century Eggs and Pork
instructions.text: Once the congee reaches your desired consistency, stir in the diced century eggs and the marinated shredded pork (if using). Cook for another 5-7 minutes, or until the pork is fully cooked through and the century eggs are heated. The congee will thicken further.

instructions.title: Season and Serve
instructions.text: Season the congee with salt and white pepper to taste. Ladle the hot congee into individual serving bowls. Garnish generously with chopped green onions and a drizzle of sesame oil. Serve immediately, optionally with a side of soy sauce for an extra savory kick.

tips: For an extra creamy congee, freeze the washed rice overnight before cooking. The freezing and thawing process breaks down the rice grains, allowing them to soften faster and achieve a smoother texture.
Ensure your century eggs are fresh and firm. To reduce the distinctive aroma, you can briefly blanch the diced century eggs in boiling water for 1-2 minutes before adding them to the congee.

Congee is best served immediately and hot. Leftovers can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat gently on the stove with a splash of water or broth to restore consistency.
article:
Start your day the traditional Chinese way – with a comforting, savory bowl of congee. More than just a simple rice porridge, congee is a staple breakfast across Asia, cherished for its nourishing qualities and incredible versatility. Among its many delightful variations, one stands out for its unique flavor profile and surprisingly creamy texture: Congee with Century Egg, often paired with shredded lean pork. This classic combination offers a symphony of tastes and textures that will awaken your palate and leave you feeling deeply satisfied. If you're looking to explore authentic Chinese breakfast recipes, diving into the world of Century Egg Congee is an absolute must. It’s a dish that embodies comfort, tradition, and culinary adventure all in one bowl.

## What is Century Egg Congee?

At its heart, Century Egg Congee is a type of *zhou* (粥), the Chinese term for rice porridge. The base is a thick, creamy porridge made from long-grain white rice, cooked down with plenty of water or broth until the grains burst and transform into a velvety smooth gruel. What makes this particular congee special, however, is the addition of century egg (皮蛋, *pídàn*).

Century eggs are a Chinese delicacy, preserved duck, chicken, or quail eggs that have been cured in a mixture of clay, ash, salt, quicklime, and rice hulls for several weeks to several months. This preservation process transforms the egg in fascinating ways: the albumen (egg white) becomes a translucent, dark brown jelly with a pattern resembling pine branches, while the yolk turns a creamy dark green or grey, often with a slightly runny center. Despite their somewhat intimidating appearance and distinctive ammonia-like aroma when first peeled, century eggs offer a complex, umami-rich flavor that is salty, earthy, and subtly pungent. When chopped and stirred into hot congee, their unique texture and taste melt into the rice porridge, creating a surprisingly harmonious and deeply savory dish. Often, shredded lean pork is also added, contributing another layer of flavor and protein, making it a hearty and complete breakfast. The combined effect is a truly memorable culinary experience, making Century Egg Congee a beloved breakfast choice.

## Ingredients You Need

Crafting a delicious bowl of Century Egg Congee requires a few key ingredients. While the process is simple, quality ingredients make all the difference.

For the Congee Base:
*   1 cup long-grain white rice (Jasmine rice is ideal)
*   10-12 cups water or chicken/pork broth (broth adds more flavor)
*   1-inch piece of ginger, sliced or smashed
*   1/2 teaspoon salt (or to taste)
*   1 tablespoon cooking oil (optional, helps prevent sticking and adds silkiness)

For the Century Egg and Pork:
*   2-3 century eggs, peeled and chopped into small cubes
*   1/2 lb lean pork loin or tenderloin, shredded or thinly sliced (optional, but highly recommended)
*   1 teaspoon soy sauce
*   1/2 teaspoon sesame oil
*   1/4 teaspoon white pepper
*   1 teaspoon cornstarch (for marinating pork)

For Garnish and Seasoning:
*   2-3 stalks green onions, chopped
*   Fresh cilantro, chopped
*   A dash of white pepper
*   A drizzle of sesame oil
*   A splash of light soy sauce (to taste)
*   Fried shallots or crispy chili oil (optional, for extra crunch and heat)

## Step-by-Step Instructions

Making Century Egg Congee is a labor of love that rewards patience with incredible flavor.

1.  **Prepare the Rice:** Rinse the rice thoroughly under cold running water until the water runs clear. For an extra creamy congee and faster cooking time, soak the rice in water for at least 30 minutes, or even overnight. Some people also like to marinate the rinsed rice with a teaspoon of oil and a pinch of salt for 15-20 minutes before cooking; this helps the grains break down more easily and prevents them from clumping.
2.  **Prepare the Pork (if using):** If you're adding pork, slice or shred the lean pork. Marinate it with soy sauce, sesame oil, white pepper, and cornstarch. Set aside.
3.  **Start the Congee:** In a large heavy-bottomed pot, combine the rinsed (and optionally soaked/marinated) rice, water or broth, and sliced ginger. Bring the mixture to a rolling boil over high heat, stirring occasionally to prevent the rice from sticking to the bottom.
4.  **Simmer and Stir:** Once boiling, reduce the heat to very low, cover the pot partially (leaving a small gap for steam to escape), and let it simmer. This is the longest step. You'll need to simmer the congee for at least 1.5 to 2 hours, or even longer, stirring every 15-20 minutes, especially towards the end, to ensure it doesn't stick and to achieve that desired creamy consistency. The rice grains should break down completely and the porridge should be thick and smooth. If it becomes too thick, add a little more hot water or broth.
5.  **Add Pork and Century Egg:** About 10-15 minutes before serving, add the marinated pork to the simmering congee. Stir gently until the pork is cooked through (it will turn opaque). Then, add the chopped century eggs. Stir them in and let them heat through for another 5 minutes.
6.  **Season and Serve:** Remove the ginger slices. Taste the Century Egg Congee and adjust seasoning with salt if needed. Ladle the hot congee into individual bowls. Garnish generously with chopped green onions, fresh cilantro, a dash of white pepper, a drizzle of sesame oil, and a splash of light soy sauce to taste. For an extra kick, add some fried shallots or chili oil.

## Pro Tips for the Best Results

Achieving that perfect bowl of congee isn't just about following steps; it's about understanding the nuances.

*   **Soak Your Rice:** This is a game-changer. Soaking rice helps it cook faster and break down more easily, resulting in a creamier, smoother congee.
*   **Use Good Broth:** While water works, a good quality chicken or pork broth will significantly elevate the flavor of your congee, adding depth and richness.
*   **Low and Slow is Key:** Patience is a virtue when making congee. Cooking it over low heat for an extended period allows the rice grains to fully disintegrate, creating that signature silky texture. Don't rush it.
*   **Stir, Stir, Stir:** Especially in the initial stages and towards the end, frequent stirring is crucial to prevent the rice from sticking to the bottom of the pot and burning. A heavy-bottomed pot also helps.
*   **Adjust Consistency:** Congee consistency is a matter of personal preference. If you like it thicker, simmer longer; if you prefer it thinner, add more hot water or broth until you reach your desired texture.
*   **Quality Century Eggs:** The taste of your Congee with Century Egg heavily relies on the quality of the century eggs. Look for eggs with firm, translucent whites and creamy, slightly runny yolks. If they have a very strong, unpleasant ammonia smell, they might not be the freshest.

## Serving Suggestions

A bowl of Century Egg Congee is wonderfully satisfying on its own, but it truly shines when accompanied by a few traditional Chinese breakfast sides and condiments.

*   **Crispy Goodness:** The ultimate pairing is *youtiao* (油条), Chinese fried dough sticks. Their crispy exterior and airy interior are perfect for dipping into the hot, savory congee, soaking up all its delicious flavors.
*   **Pickled Vegetables:** A small plate of pickled daikon, cucumbers, or mustard greens offers a refreshing crunch and tangy counterpoint that cuts through the richness of the congee.
*   **Other Dim Sum:** For a more elaborate breakfast spread, consider serving your congee alongside steamed dumplings, spring rolls, or turnip cake.
*   **Condiments Galore:** Encourage diners to customize their bowl! Offer extra soy sauce, white pepper, sesame oil, and especially chili oil for those who enjoy a bit of heat. Crispy fried shallots or garlic flakes also add a lovely aromatic crunch.
*   **Aromatic Herbs:** Don't skimp on the fresh green onions and cilantro. Their vibrant freshness brightens up every spoonful.

## Variations and Substitutions

The beauty of congee lies in its adaptability. Once you've mastered the classic Century Egg Congee, feel free to experiment with these variations:

*   **Plain Congee (White Congee):** For a simpler, more delicate breakfast, omit the century egg and pork. Serve plain congee with a variety of toppings on the side, like pickled tofu, fermented bean curd, or roasted peanuts.
*   **Different Proteins:** Instead of pork, you can use shredded chicken, thinly sliced fish, or even ground beef. Marinate them similarly to the pork before adding.
*   **Salted Duck Egg:** Often served alongside or in place of century egg, salted duck eggs (咸鸭蛋, *xiányādàn*) add a different kind of salty, rich flavor. Their bright orange yolks are particularly prized.
*   **Vegetarian Options:** For a vegetarian version, omit the pork and use vegetable broth. You can add sliced mushrooms (shiitake or oyster), tofu cubes, or even goji berries for a different nutritional profile.
*   **Pressure Cooker Method:** If you're short on time, a pressure cooker can significantly reduce the cooking time. Combine rice and liquid, cook on high pressure for 20-25 minutes, then allow natural release. The result is still wonderfully creamy.
*   **Leftover Rice:** You can even make congee with leftover cooked rice, though it might require a bit more liquid and a slightly longer cooking time to achieve the desired breakdown of grains.

Mastering Century Egg Congee is a rewarding culinary journey that introduces you to the heart of Chinese breakfast. Its soothing warmth, complex flavors, and customizable nature make it a dish you'll want to revisit again and again. So, gather your ingredients, set aside some time, and embark on the delicious adventure of making this traditional Chinese comfort food. Your taste buds will thank you!
